cultural.summary: Remove sick plants right away so the Vata imbalance doesn't spread!
cultural.how: Remove and destroy entire plant immediately on symptom appearance.

cultural.summary: Hang yellow sticky cards near the plant canopy to catch sap-sucking whiteflies.
cultural.how: Hang near plant canopy to monitor and trap whitefly vectors.

cultural.summary: Boost seed immunity right from the start using local Himachal methods!
cultural.how: Soak seeds in cow urine before sowing, especially for kharif-season crops.

biological.summary: A powerful classical fermented tonic of dairy and cow urine to restore root strength.
biological.how: Ferment cow milk, curd, ghee, cow urine, and cow dung. Dilute and irrigate the root zone.

biological.summary: Purify the air around the leaves using traditional Ayurvedic fumigation.
biological.how: Burn dried neem leaves near the plant and allow the smoke to pass near the foliage.

biological.summary: Soapy neem bath prevents whiteflies from spreading the curl virus.
biological.how: Mix 5 ml neem oil with a couple of drops of liquid soap in 1 litre water. Spray whole plant.

cultural.summary: A simple, local Himachal trick to dry out fungi around the roots!
cultural.how: Dust wood ash directly around the base of the plant.

botanical.summary: Use fallen pine needles as a protective mulch layer over the soil.
botanical.how: Spread Pinus roxburgii needles around the base of the plant, 5-7cm thick.

biological.summary: A soothing classical Pitta-balancing decoction to cool the plant's system.
biological.how: Prepare a decoction of Yashtimadhu (licorice root) and Madhuca, mix with milk and honey, and irrigate.

biological.summary: A local farm-made pesticide paste applied right to the soil.
biological.how: Mix cow dung with water and apply to the plant/soil as a natural pesticide.

cultural.summary: Give plants plenty of personal space to dry out excess Kapha moisture.
cultural.how: Ensure adequate spacing at planting for maximum airflow.

botanical.summary: A clever local trick from Bilaspur to trap pests using fermented dairy!
botanical.how: Set out containers of buttermilk around the crop to act as local pest traps.

biological.summary: Diluted milk under morning sun creates a natural antiseptic action against white mildew.
biological.how: Mix 1 part milk with 9 parts water. Spray on leaves in morning sunlight.

cultural.summary: Beautiful marigold roots naturally repel hidden nematodes!
cultural.how: Plant marigolds near or before transplanting tomatoes.

botanical.summary: Enrich the soil with bitter neem cake to make it hostile for root worms.
botanical.how: Mix neem cake into the soil before planting.
botanical.frequency: Once at planting, refresh every 2-3 months

biological.summary: A classical shock-and-heal treatment for infested root zones.
biological.how: Irrigate with cold water for 7 consecutive days, then apply a cow dung, water, and milk paste to roots.

biological.summary: A potent Ayurvedic herbal paste applied directly to affected plant parts.
biological.how: Combine white mustard, Vacha, and Kushta into a paste. Apply directly to affected root/plant part.

cultural.summary: Protect stems from tools and heavy wind to prevent pathogen entry points.
cultural.how: Handle plants gently during pruning and weeding.

biological.summary: A classical Ayurvedic band-aid for cracked or wounded stems!
biological.how: Combine banyan bark, cluster fig bark, cow dung, honey, and ghee into a paste. Apply directly to the wound.
biological.frequency: Once, or as needed until healed

cultural.summary: The germ lives in the soil and spreads through water and tools, so a wilted plant must go before it infects its neighbours.
cultural.how: Uproot the whole plant with its roots and a ball of soil as soon as it wilts. Burn it or bury it deep; do not compost it. Wash tools and boots before moving to healthy plants.

cultural.summary: A quick way to confirm bacterial wilt before you pull out more plants.
cultural.how: Cut a piece of the lower stem and hang it in a glass of clear water. If milky white threads stream out of the cut end within a few minutes, it is bacterial wilt.

cultural.summary: The germ survives in the soil for years, so growing something it cannot infect starves it out.
cultural.how: Keep tomato, potato, brinjal and capsicum out of an infected plot for at least 3-4 seasons. Grow maize, cabbage-family crops, onion or legumes there instead.

cultural.summary: The disease explodes in saturated soil at 30-35 °C, and flowing water carries the germs between plants.
cultural.how: Plant on raised beds with drainage channels, irrigate lightly, and never let irrigation or rain water run from an infected plot into a healthy one. Avoid hoeing close to the roots.

cultural.summary: The disease develops fastest in acidic soil (below pH 6), and lime gave one of the biggest yield gains in ICAR field trials.
cultural.how: Get the soil pH tested and work agricultural lime into acidic soil about 15 days before transplanting, at the rate your local soil test or KVK advises.

cultural.summary: Planting an infected seedling brings the disease into a clean field.
cultural.how: Raise seedlings in a fresh nursery bed or trays with clean soil or compost, away from any plot that had wilt, and discard any seedling that looks weak or wilted.

botanical.summary: Neem cake is part of the standard integrated programme for this disease.
botanical.how: Apply neem cake at about 100 kg per acre, mixed into the soil before transplanting.

botanical.summary: In ICAR field trials, karanj cake gave the best plant survival of all the soil treatments tried.
botanical.how: Mix karanj cake into the soil about 15 days before transplanting, in the same quantity you would use for neem cake.

biological.summary: Friendly soil microbes (Trichoderma, Pseudomonas fluorescens) crowd out the wilt bacteria around the roots and are part of ICAR's integrated trials.
biological.how: Mix the culture into well-rotted farmyard manure at the dose on the product pack, keep it moist in shade for about a week, then apply it to the soil.

biological.action: Graft on a Wild Brinjal Rootstock
biological.summary: Tomato grafted on wilt-tolerant wild brinjal (Solanum torvum) kept far more plants alive in Indian trials, though it does not make them immune.
biological.how: Use grafted seedlings from a nursery or the horticulture department for plots known to carry bacterial wilt.

cultural.summary: The fungus starts on the lowest leaves, splashed up from the soil. In HP trials at Palampur, staking with lower-leaf removal lowered disease.
cultural.how: Tie plants to stakes and remove the spotted and ground-touching leaves on a dry day. Bag them and take them out of the field.

cultural.summary: Wider row spacing reduced severity in HP field trials because leaves dry faster.
cultural.how: Keep to the wider end of the recommended spacing, and avoid working among wet plants.

cultural.summary: A 2-4 inch layer of mulch blocks the splash that carries spores from soil to leaves.
cultural.how: After transplanting, spread straw, dry grass or pine needles 5-10 cm thick over the soil, keeping it off the stems.

cultural.action: Water the Roots, Not the Leaves
cultural.summary: The spots need long leaf wetness to develop.
cultural.how: Water the soil at the base in the morning so leaves dry quickly.

cultural.summary: The fungus winters on old debris and on wild nightshade-family weeds.
cultural.how: Do not grow tomato or potato in the same plot for 3-4 years, pull out nightshade weeds and, after harvest, remove plant debris and plough the rest in.

cultural.summary: In HP trials, tomato intercropped with maize had less leaf spot than with beans or toria.
cultural.how: Where space allows, grow maize rows alongside tomato instead of beans or mustard.

biological.summary: Foliar sprays of Trichoderma viride or T. harzianum reduced Septoria in hill-region trials, though less than chemical fungicide, so combine with the cultural steps.
biological.how: Mix the Trichoderma powder in clean water at the dose on the product pack and spray both sides of the leaves in the evening.
